question: A solutions architect adds a shell script to the user data of a Linux EC2 instance to install and start a web server. By default, when does this user data script run?
options: Only when an administrator runs it through AWS Systems Manager
Every time the instance is rebooted
Only during the first boot cycle after the instance is launched
Every time the instance is stopped and started
explanation: By default, cloud-init runs user data scripts once, as the root user, during the first boot of a newly launched instance. Reboots and stop/start cycles do not rerun the script unless it is explicitly configured to run on every boot. Systems Manager is not needed to execute user data.

question: An Auto Scaling group launches instances that run a user data script to install packages, download application binaries, and compile dependencies. Each new instance takes 18 minutes to become ready, so the group cannot react quickly to traffic spikes. Which solution will MOST reduce the time for new instances to become ready?
options: Create a pre-baked golden AMI that already contains the software and keep only instance-specific configuration in user data
Move the user data script into a CloudFormation cfn-init configuration
Increase the health check grace period of the Auto Scaling group
Use larger instance types so that the script runs faster
explanation: Baking software into a golden AMI moves the slow installation work to build time, so new instances only perform small final configuration steps and become ready quickly. cfn-init still performs the same installation at boot. A longer grace period only delays health checks and does not speed up readiness. Larger instances may shorten compilation slightly, but downloads and installs still dominate and the instances cost more.

question: A developer passes a database password to an EC2 instance in its user data so that a startup script can configure the application. A security engineer flags this as a risk. What is the risk, and what should be done instead?
options: User data is encrypted with the instance's KMS key, so the only risk is its size; compress the script instead

User data can be read by any process on the instance through the metadata service and by anyone allowed to view instance attributes; retrieve the password at runtime from AWS Secrets Manager by using the instance role
User data is published on the internet; move the instance to a private subnet
User data is deleted after boot, so the application will lose the password; store it in an environment variable baked into the AMI
explanation: User data is not encrypted and can be retrieved from the instance metadata service by any local process and through the DescribeInstanceAttribute API, so it must not contain secrets. The instance should use its IAM role to fetch the secret from Secrets Manager at runtime. User data is not published on the internet and is not deleted after boot, and baking secrets into an AMI is also insecure.

question: A team manages EC2 instances with AWS CloudFormation. Their long user data scripts are difficult to maintain and do not clearly express the desired state of packages, files, and services. Which approach provides a declarative way to configure the instances from the template?
options: Use the CloudFormation DependsOn attribute to install packages in order
Store the scripts in a CloudFormation stack policy
Use CloudFormation drift detection to apply package changes
Define the configuration in the AWS::CloudFormation::Init metadata of the instance resource and run cfn-init from user data
explanation: AWS::CloudFormation::Init metadata declares packages, groups, users, sources, files, commands, and services, and the cfn-init helper script reads that metadata and applies it on the instance. DependsOn only controls the order in which resources are created. Stack policies protect resources from updates. Drift detection reports differences but does not configure instances.

question: A CloudFormation stack creates an EC2 instance and then other resources that depend on it. The stack reports CREATE_COMPLETE as soon as the instance is running, even though the application installation in user data often fails. The company wants the stack to succeed only if the application is configured correctly. Which solution meets this requirement?
options: Enable termination protection on the stack
Add an UpdatePolicy with AutoScalingRollingUpdate to the instance resource
Add a DeletionPolicy of Retain to the instance resource
Add a CreationPolicy to the instance and run cfn-signal at the end of the user data script with the exit status of the installation
explanation: A CreationPolicy makes CloudFormation wait for a success signal, and cfn-signal reports the result of the installation; if a failure signal is sent or the timeout expires, resource creation fails and the stack rolls back. DeletionPolicy controls what happens to resources when they are deleted. Stack termination protection prevents stack deletion. UpdatePolicy applies to updates of Auto Scaling groups, not to the creation of an individual instance.

question: A CloudFormation template creates an Auto Scaling group with a desired capacity of 4. The stack must not reach CREATE_COMPLETE until 4 instances have finished bootstrapping, and stack creation must fail if this does not happen within 15 minutes. Which configuration meets these requirements?
options: Add a WaitCondition with a Count of 1 and a Timeout of 15 minutes
Set the HealthCheckGracePeriod of the Auto Scaling group to 900 seconds
Add a CreationPolicy to the Auto Scaling group with a ResourceSignal Count of 4 and a Timeout of PT15M, and run cfn-signal on each instance
Add a DependsOn attribute that references the launch template
explanation: A CreationPolicy on the Auto Scaling group with a ResourceSignal Count of 4 and a Timeout of PT15M makes CloudFormation wait for four success signals sent by cfn-signal, and creation fails if they do not arrive in time. A WaitCondition with a Count of 1 completes after a single signal. The health check grace period affects Auto Scaling health checks, not stack completion. DependsOn only orders resource creation.

question: A company uses cfn-init and AWS::CloudFormation::Init metadata to configure EC2 instances. When an engineer changes a configuration file in the metadata and updates the stack, the running instances do not pick up the change. The company wants running instances to apply metadata changes automatically without being replaced. What should a solutions architect configure?
options: Run CloudFormation drift detection on a schedule
Run the cfn-hup daemon on the instances with a hook that reruns cfn-init when the metadata changes
Add a CreationPolicy with a longer timeout
Configure the user data to run on every boot and reboot the instances after each update
explanation: cfn-hup polls the resource metadata for changes and runs configured hooks, typically cfn-init, when it detects an update, so running instances apply the new configuration in place. A CreationPolicy only affects signaling during initial creation. Rebooting with every-boot user data is disruptive and manual. Drift detection identifies differences but does not apply configuration.

question: A company must provide hardened, fully patched AMIs every month to development teams in multiple accounts and Regions. Each AMI must pass security tests before it is distributed. The company wants a managed solution with the LEAST operational overhead. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Create an EC2 Image Builder pipeline with build and test components, a monthly schedule, and a distribution configuration for the target Regions and accounts
Use AWS Compute Optimizer to recommend updated AMIs every month
Run a scheduled script on a build instance that patches it, creates an AMI, and copies the AMI to other Regions
Use AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager to patch the running instances in each account
explanation: EC2 Image Builder automates building, hardening, and testing images on a schedule and distributes the resulting AMIs to multiple Regions and accounts through its distribution settings, with no custom build tooling to maintain. A custom script can work but requires maintenance and lacks built-in testing. Patch Manager patches running instances rather than producing images. Compute Optimizer provides right-sizing recommendations, not AMIs.

question: An EC2 Image Builder pipeline produces a new AMI every week. After two years, the account holds hundreds of outdated AMIs and snapshots, which increases storage costs. The company wants to keep only the five most recent images and remove older ones automatically. Which solution requires the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Write a Lambda function that deregisters old AMIs and deletes their snapshots on a schedule
Configure an EC2 Image Builder lifecycle policy that retains the five most recent images and deletes older AMIs and their snapshots
Move all of the AMI snapshots to the EBS Snapshots Archive tier
Create a Recycle Bin retention rule for AMIs with a 7-day retention period
explanation: Image Builder lifecycle policies can automatically deprecate, disable, or delete older images, including their AMIs and snapshots, based on count or age rules, without custom code. A Lambda function works but must be written and maintained. Archiving lowers cost but still keeps every outdated snapshot. Recycle Bin only retains resources after deletion and does not remove anything.

question: An application on an EC2 instance needs to read objects from an Amazon S3 bucket. What is the MOST secure way to provide AWS credentials to the application?
options: Embed the root user access keys in the AMI
Pass access keys to the instance in user data
Create an IAM user, generate access keys, and store them in the application configuration file
Attach an IAM role with the required S3 permissions to the instance through an instance profile
explanation: An IAM role attached through an instance profile delivers temporary credentials that are rotated automatically and retrieved by the SDK from instance metadata, so no long-lived keys exist on the instance. Access keys in configuration files, AMIs, or user data are long-lived and can leak, and root user access keys should never be used for applications.

question: An engineer creates an IAM role for EC2 with the AWS CLI and then tries to attach it when launching an instance, but the role cannot be selected. The same process works when the role is created in the IAM console. What is the cause?
options: No instance profile was created and the role was not added to one, which the console does automatically
The role's trust policy must allow lambda.amazonaws.com
Roles created with the AWS CLI can be used only by Lambda functions
The role must be tagged with the ID of the instance that will use it
explanation: EC2 attaches roles through an instance profile, which is a container for a single role. The IAM console automatically creates an instance profile with the same name when you create a role for EC2, but with the CLI or API you must call CreateInstanceProfile and AddRoleToInstanceProfile yourself. The trust policy must allow ec2.amazonaws.com, not Lambda, and roles do not need instance ID tags.

question: How does an application running on an EC2 instance with an attached IAM role obtain AWS credentials when it uses the AWS SDK?
options: The SDK calls AWS STS AssumeRole with access keys stored in user data
The SDK reads long-lived access keys that AWS writes to the instance's home directory
The SDK retrieves temporary security credentials from the instance metadata service, and AWS rotates them automatically before they expire
The SDK requests a password from AWS IAM Identity Center for each API call
explanation: The SDK default credential provider chain retrieves temporary credentials for the instance role from the instance metadata service, and AWS rotates these credentials automatically before they expire. No long-lived keys are written to disk, IAM Identity Center is used for workforce sign-in, and no stored keys are needed to use the role.

question: A running production EC2 instance needs additional permissions to send messages to an Amazon SQS queue. The instance already has an instance profile whose role grants S3 access. The company cannot tolerate downtime. What is the simplest way to grant the new permission?
options: Launch a new instance with a new role and migrate the application to it
Store SQS-specific access keys in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store and update the application to use them
Stop the instance, attach a different instance profile, and start the instance
Add a policy that allows the required SQS actions to the role that is already attached to the instance
explanation: Permissions added to the existing role apply to the instance without a restart, because the instance uses temporary credentials for that role and IAM evaluates the role's current policies on each request. Even replacing the instance profile does not require stopping the instance, so a stop is unnecessary. Launching a new instance adds work and risk, and long-lived access keys are less secure than role credentials.

question: An application on EC2 connects to an Amazon RDS for MySQL database. The security team requires the database password to be rotated automatically every 30 days, and the application must not need code changes after each rotation. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Store the password in AWS Secrets Manager with managed rotation enabled, and have the application retrieve the secret at runtime
Store the password in an encrypted S3 object and rotate it manually
Store the password in user data and update the launch template every month
Store the password as a SecureString parameter in Parameter Store and write a cron job that changes it
explanation: AWS Secrets Manager provides built-in scheduled rotation for Amazon RDS credentials, and the application retrieves the current value at runtime, so nothing changes in the code after rotation. Parameter Store SecureString parameters have no native rotation and would require custom automation. Manual rotation in S3 or through user data adds work and exposes the secret.

question: A company needs a central place to store about 300 non-secret configuration values, such as feature flags and endpoint URLs, for applications running on EC2. Values must be versioned and accessible through IAM-controlled API calls. Which option is the MOST cost-effective?
options: An Amazon RDS table that each application queries
AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store standard parameters
An Amazon DynamoDB table with provisioned capacity
AWS Secrets Manager secrets
explanation: Parameter Store standard parameters have no storage charge, support versioning and IAM access control, and are designed for configuration data. Secrets Manager charges per secret per month and is intended for secrets that need rotation or cross-Region replication. Running a database or a provisioned DynamoDB table for configuration adds cost and management.

question: A company stores application configuration in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store under paths such as /payments/prod/ and /payments/dev/. Production instances must be able to read only production parameters, and the database connection string must be encrypted. Which actions should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)
options: Grant the production instance role ssm:GetParametersByPath and ssm:GetParameter only on the /payments/prod/ path, plus kms:Decrypt on the key
Store all parameters as String parameters and enable S3 default encryption
Place production and development parameters in separate Regions to isolate them
Grant the production instance role ssm:* on all parameters and rely on naming conventions
Store the connection string as a SecureString parameter encrypted with an AWS KMS key
explanation: SecureString parameters are encrypted with AWS KMS, and IAM policies can restrict access to a parameter hierarchy path, with kms:Decrypt required to read the decrypted value. String parameters are not encrypted, and S3 encryption has nothing to do with Parameter Store. Separate Regions add complexity without enforcing least privilege, and ssm:* on all parameters violates least privilege.

question: A company runs its application in us-east-1 with a warm standby in eu-west-1. The application retrieves database credentials from AWS Secrets Manager. During a Regional failover, the standby must be able to read the same secret locally even if us-east-1 is unavailable, and the value must stay in sync after rotation. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Configure the standby application to call the us-east-1 Secrets Manager endpoint
Store the credentials in the AMI used in eu-west-1
Replicate the secret to eu-west-1 with Secrets Manager multi-Region secret replication so that the replica is updated when the primary secret is rotated
Copy the secret value to Parameter Store in eu-west-1 with a scheduled Lambda function
explanation: Secrets Manager can replicate a secret to other Regions and keeps the replica's value in sync with the primary, including after rotation, so the standby can read it locally. A custom Lambda copy adds code and risks drift. Calling the us-east-1 endpoint fails if that Region is unavailable. Credentials baked into an AMI are insecure and quickly become stale.

question: A company stores configuration in Parameter Store. One parameter must hold a 6 KB JSON document, and several temporary access tokens must be removed automatically 24 hours after they are created. The company wants to keep costs as low as possible for its many other small parameters. Which approach meets these requirements?
options: Move all of the parameters to AWS Secrets Manager
Change every parameter in the account to the advanced tier
Keep all parameters in the standard tier and delete the expired tokens manually
Use advanced-tier parameters only for the 6 KB document and for the tokens with an Expiration parameter policy, and keep the other parameters in the standard tier
explanation: Standard parameters are limited to 4 KB and do not support parameter policies, while advanced parameters allow values up to 8 KB and policies such as Expiration but are charged per parameter. Using the advanced tier only where it is needed minimizes cost. Moving everything to Secrets Manager or to the advanced tier adds charges for parameters that do not need those features, and manual deletion adds operational effort and does not fit the 6 KB value in the standard tier.

question: A company wants to remove SSH access from its EC2 fleet. Administrators still need interactive shell access, and every session must be auditable. Which benefits does AWS Systems Manager Session Manager provide for this requirement? (Select TWO.)
options: Instances do not need any inbound ports open in their security groups
A bastion host is deployed automatically in each VPC to broker sessions
Sessions can be opened only to instances that have public IP addresses
Session activity can be logged to Amazon S3 or CloudWatch Logs, and session API calls are recorded in AWS CloudTrail
Each administrator authenticates with a personal SSH key pair stored by Session Manager
explanation: The SSM Agent opens outbound connections to the service, so Session Manager needs no inbound ports, bastion hosts, or SSH keys, and access is controlled with IAM. Session output can be logged to S3 or CloudWatch Logs, and the API calls are recorded in CloudTrail. It works for instances in private subnets through a NAT gateway or VPC endpoints, not only for public instances.

question: EC2 instances in a private subnet have no internet access and no NAT gateway. The instances run the SSM Agent and have an instance profile with the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy, but they do not appear as managed nodes in Systems Manager. Which interface VPC endpoints should be created so that administrators can use Session Manager? (Select THREE.)
options: com.amazonaws.region.sts
com.amazonaws.region.ec2messages
com.amazonaws.region.ssmmessages
com.amazonaws.region.ec2
com.amazonaws.region.ssm
com.amazonaws.region.kinesis-streams
explanation: Systems Manager guidance for private subnets without internet access calls for interface endpoints for ssm, ssmmessages, and ec2messages; ssmmessages carries the Session Manager data channel and the others carry agent communication with the service. The ec2 endpoint is needed only for certain other features, and Kinesis and STS endpoints are not required for Session Manager connectivity.

question: An operations team must restart a service and collect a diagnostic file on 400 EC2 instances tagged Role=api, without opening SSH, and must avoid affecting more than 10% of the fleet at a time. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Update the user data of each instance and reboot all of the instances
Build a new AMI with the fix and replace all of the instances at once
Use AWS Systems Manager Run Command to target the tag with a concurrency limit of 10% and an error threshold
Write a script that loops through the instances and connects to them with SSH in batches
explanation: Run Command executes documents on managed instances selected by tags, with rate controls for concurrency and error thresholds, and requires no inbound SSH. An SSH loop needs open ports, keys, and custom scripting. Changing user data and rebooting does not rerun the commands by default and disrupts the fleet. Replacing all instances at once violates the 10% limit.

question: A company must automatically install security updates on its Amazon Linux and Windows EC2 instances every Sunday at 02:00 and must approve only critical and important security patches 7 days after their release. Which AWS Systems Manager configuration should a solutions architect use? (Select TWO.)
options: Use AWS Config to install missing patches when instances become noncompliant
Create a maintenance window scheduled for Sunday at 02:00 that runs the AWS-RunPatchBaseline document against the instances
Use Session Manager to connect to each instance and run the update commands manually
Create custom patch baselines with auto-approval rules for critical and important security patches after 7 days
Use EC2 Image Builder to patch the running instances in place
explanation: Patch baselines define which patches are approved, including severity filters and auto-approval delays, and a maintenance window schedules AWS-RunPatchBaseline to scan for and install those patches at the required time. Manual Session Manager work does not scale. AWS Config evaluates compliance but does not install patches by itself, and Image Builder builds new images rather than patching running instances.

question: A newly launched EC2 instance does not appear as a managed node in AWS Systems Manager. The instance has outbound internet access through a NAT gateway. Which requirements must be met for the instance to be managed by Systems Manager? (Select TWO.)
options: The SSM Agent must be installed and running on the instance
The instance must have IAM permissions for Systems Manager, such as an instance profile that includes AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore
The instance must have an Elastic IP address
The instance must run on a Dedicated Host
The security group must allow inbound TCP port 22 from the Systems Manager service
explanation: Systems Manager requires the SSM Agent on the instance and IAM permissions that let the agent communicate with the service, typically through an instance profile with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore. The agent makes outbound connections, so no inbound ports or Elastic IP addresses are needed, and tenancy does not matter.

question: A solutions architect wants to create an alarm when memory utilization on Linux EC2 instances exceeds 85%, but cannot find a memory utilization metric in the AWS/EC2 namespace. What is the reason?
options: EC2 does not publish operating system memory metrics by default, so the CloudWatch agent must be installed to collect them
Memory metrics are published only for instances that have instance store volumes
Memory metrics appear only after an instance has been running for 24 hours
Memory metrics are available only when detailed monitoring is enabled
explanation: The hypervisor cannot see memory usage inside the guest operating system, so EC2 does not publish memory utilization by default; the CloudWatch agent collects it from inside the OS and publishes it as a custom metric, by default in the CWAgent namespace. Detailed monitoring only increases the frequency of the default metrics. Storage type and uptime do not affect memory metrics.

question: A company must deploy the same CloudWatch agent configuration, which collects memory, disk, and application log data, to 1,500 EC2 instances and must be able to update it centrally. Which approach requires the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Bake the configuration into the AMI and replace the instances whenever it changes
Store the agent configuration in Systems Manager Parameter Store and use Systems Manager to install and configure the agent across the fleet
Configure the agent on each instance manually through the CloudWatch console
Copy the configuration file to each instance with SCP after every change
explanation: The CloudWatch agent can load its configuration from a Parameter Store parameter, and Systems Manager Run Command or State Manager can install and apply that configuration across the fleet, so updates are made once centrally. Manual copying or per-instance configuration does not scale. Rebuilding AMIs and replacing instances for each configuration change adds significant effort.

question: A web application on EC2 crashed when its root file system filled up. The company wants to be notified before disk usage on the file system exceeds 80%. Which actions should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)
options: Install the CloudWatch agent and configure it to collect the disk used_percent metric for the file system
Create a CloudWatch alarm on the agent's disk used_percent metric that publishes to an Amazon SNS topic
Use the EBSWriteBytes metric to estimate the remaining free space
Enable Fast Snapshot Restore for the root volume's snapshots
Enable detailed monitoring on the instance to publish file system utilization
explanation: File system usage is visible only from inside the operating system, so the CloudWatch agent must collect the disk used_percent metric, and a CloudWatch alarm on that metric can notify an Amazon SNS topic. Detailed monitoring only increases the frequency of standard metrics and does not add file system usage. EBSWriteBytes measures I/O, not free space, and Fast Snapshot Restore is unrelated.

question: An application on a fleet of EC2 instances writes errors to /var/log/app/error.log. When Auto Scaling terminates instances, their logs are lost. The company also wants an alarm when more than 50 errors occur within 5 minutes. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Store the log file on an instance store volume and copy it to Amazon S3 when the instance stops
Enable VPC Flow Logs and create an alarm on rejected connections
Enable detailed monitoring and create an alarm on the StatusCheckFailed metric
Configure the CloudWatch agent to send the log file to CloudWatch Logs, create a metric filter for error entries, and create an alarm on the resulting metric
explanation: The CloudWatch agent streams log files to CloudWatch Logs so they persist after instances terminate, and a metric filter turns matching log events into a metric that can trigger an alarm. Instance store data is lost at termination, and a scale-in event may not leave time to copy files. VPC Flow Logs capture network traffic, not application errors. Status check metrics do not reflect application errors.

question: A company runs a tightly coupled high performance computing job that requires the lowest possible network latency and the highest packet-per-second throughput between nodes. Which placement strategy should be used?
options: A partition placement group with seven partitions
A cluster placement group in a single Availability Zone
No placement group, with instances distributed across several subnets
A spread placement group across three Availability Zones
explanation: A cluster placement group packs instances close together within one Availability Zone to deliver low latency and high network throughput, which suits tightly coupled HPC. Spread and partition placement groups distribute instances across hardware to reduce correlated failures, which works against minimum latency. Distributing instances without a placement group also increases latency.

question: A company runs six critical instances that form a small quorum-based cluster. Each instance must run on distinct underlying hardware to minimize the risk of simultaneous failures, and all instances must stay in a single Availability Zone because of a licensing restriction. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Launch the instances as Dedicated Instances without a placement group
Launch the instances in a cluster placement group
Launch the instances in a spread placement group
Launch the instances on a single Dedicated Host
explanation: A spread placement group places each instance on a distinct rack with its own network and power source and supports up to seven running instances per Availability Zone, which fits six instances in one AZ. A cluster placement group places instances close together and increases correlated failure risk. A single Dedicated Host is one physical server, and Dedicated Instances without a placement group do not guarantee distinct hardware.

question: A company is deploying a 90-node Apache Cassandra cluster on EC2. The database is rack-aware and needs to know which instances share underlying hardware so that replicas can be placed in different failure domains. Which placement strategy meets these requirements?
options: A partition placement group, with each instance reading its partition number from instance metadata
Random placement across subnets in one Availability Zone
A cluster placement group
A spread placement group
explanation: Partition placement groups divide instances into logical partitions that do not share racks, support hundreds of instances, and expose each instance's partition number through instance metadata, so rack-aware software such as Cassandra, HDFS, or Kafka can place replicas correctly. A spread placement group is limited to seven running instances per Availability Zone. A cluster placement group concentrates failure risk, and random placement gives no visibility into hardware topology.

question: A team launched 4 instances into a cluster placement group and later tries to add 12 more instances of a different instance type. The launch fails with an insufficient capacity error. What is the recommended way to avoid this problem?
options: Launch all of the required instances in a single launch request and use the same instance type for every instance in the placement group
Change the strategy of the existing placement group from cluster to spread
Extend the cluster placement group into a second Availability Zone
Attach smaller EBS volumes to the new instances
explanation: AWS recommends launching all the instances you need in a single launch request and using the same instance type, because adding instances later or mixing types increases the chance of insufficient capacity errors in a cluster placement group; stopping and starting all instances in the group can also help. A spread placement group would remove the low-latency benefit, a cluster placement group cannot span Availability Zones, and EBS volume size has no effect on host capacity.

question: A company must run 24 instances of a distributed application in one Availability Zone. The instances must be grouped so that a single rack failure affects at most one group, and the application needs to know which group each instance belongs to. Which placement group configuration meets these requirements?
options: A single spread placement group that contains all 24 instances
A partition placement group with multiple partitions
A cluster placement group that contains all 24 instances
Three spread placement groups with eight instances each
explanation: A partition placement group in one Availability Zone supports up to seven partitions, each on its own set of racks, with many instances per partition, and each instance can read its partition number from instance metadata. A spread placement group allows at most seven running instances per Availability Zone, so neither one group of 24 nor groups of eight would work. A cluster placement group concentrates instances on nearby hardware, which increases correlated failure risk.

question: Which EC2 feature uses single root I/O virtualization (SR-IOV) to provide higher bandwidth, higher packet-per-second performance, and lower latency at no additional charge on supported instance types?
options: EC2 Instance Connect
VPC Flow Logs
Enhanced networking with the Elastic Network Adapter (ENA)
Elastic IP addresses
explanation: Enhanced networking uses SR-IOV, most commonly through the Elastic Network Adapter, to deliver high throughput, high packets per second, and consistently low latency on supported instance types with no extra charge. Elastic IP addresses provide static public addresses, EC2 Instance Connect handles SSH access, and Flow Logs capture traffic metadata.

question: A research institute runs a weather model that uses MPI across hundreds of nodes, and inter-node communication latency limits how far the model can scale. The team wants inter-node communication to bypass the operating system kernel on supported Linux instances. Which solution meets this requirement?
options: Enable EBS optimization on every node
Place the nodes in a spread placement group across multiple Availability Zones
Attach several ENA interfaces to each instance and bond them together
Use an Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) on supported instance types with an MPI library configured to use it
explanation: An Elastic Fabric Adapter provides OS-bypass capabilities so that MPI and NCCL applications communicate directly with the network hardware, giving lower and more consistent latency than TCP over ENA for tightly coupled HPC and ML workloads. Bonding ENA interfaces still uses the kernel network stack. EBS optimization affects storage traffic, and spreading nodes across Availability Zones increases latency.

question: A company is building a cluster of EC2 instances for computational fluid dynamics simulations that are tightly coupled and very sensitive to network latency between nodes. Which actions should a solutions architect take to achieve the BEST network performance? (Select TWO.)
options: Route node-to-node traffic through a Network Load Balancer
Use instance types that support Elastic Fabric Adapter and attach an EFA to each instance
Distribute the instances across three Availability Zones for resilience
Launch the instances in a cluster placement group
Use a partition placement group with one instance in each partition
explanation: A cluster placement group keeps nodes physically close in one Availability Zone for low latency and high bandwidth, and EFA adds OS-bypass networking for MPI traffic. Spreading instances across Availability Zones or partitions increases the distance between nodes and therefore latency. Placing a load balancer between nodes adds hops and does not suit peer-to-peer MPI traffic.

question: On a busy database server, heavy network traffic from application clients competes with traffic to the instance's EBS volumes, which causes inconsistent storage latency. What does an EBS-optimized instance provide to address this problem?
options: Local NVMe storage that replaces the EBS volumes
Dedicated bandwidth between the instance and Amazon EBS that is separate from other network traffic
Automatic conversion of gp3 volumes to io2 volumes
Fast Snapshot Restore for all attached volumes at no charge
explanation: EBS-optimized instances provide dedicated capacity for EBS I/O, so storage traffic does not contend with the instance's other network traffic and EBS performance is more consistent; most current-generation instance types are EBS-optimized by default. EBS optimization does not replace EBS with local storage, change volume types, or enable Fast Snapshot Restore.

question: A database runs on an m6i.large instance with an io2 volume provisioned for 30,000 IOPS. During nightly loads that last several hours, the volume reaches its provisioned IOPS for roughly the first 30 minutes and then drops to a much lower level for the rest of the load, with a high queue length. Which change will MOST likely resolve this?
options: Enable Multi-Attach on the io2 volume so that it can reach its provisioned IOPS
Enable Fast Snapshot Restore on the snapshot that the volume was created from
Move to a larger instance size whose baseline EBS IOPS and bandwidth meet the volume's provisioned performance
Increase the size of the io2 volume beyond 16 TiB
explanation: Smaller instance sizes have a baseline EBS bandwidth and IOPS limit and can burst to their maximum only for a limited time each day, so the instance, not the volume, becomes the bottleneck once the burst is used up. An instance size whose baseline EBS performance covers 30,000 IOPS removes the limit. Multi-Attach shares a volume and does not raise performance, Fast Snapshot Restore only affects initialization after a restore, and io2 IOPS do not depend on the volume being larger than 16 TiB.

question: An application uses 150 non-sensitive configuration values and 4 database credentials. The credentials must be rotated automatically, and the company wants to minimize cost. Which storage choices meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
options: Store the 150 configuration values as Parameter Store standard parameters
Store all of the values in EC2 user data
Store the 4 database credentials in AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation
Store the 150 configuration values as AWS Secrets Manager secrets
Store the 4 database credentials as plaintext String parameters in Parameter Store
explanation: Parameter Store standard parameters have no storage charge, which makes them the cost-effective choice for non-sensitive configuration, while Secrets Manager provides automatic rotation for database credentials at a small per-secret monthly charge. Storing 150 configuration values in Secrets Manager adds unnecessary monthly cost. Plaintext String parameters and user data neither protect nor rotate credentials.

question: A company runs a bastion host with an Elastic IP address in each of three Availability Zones only to give administrators SSH access to private instances. The company wants to reduce cost and operational effort while keeping access auditable. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager to connect to the private instances and terminate the bastion hosts
Move the private instances to public subnets and restrict SSH by source IP address
Replace the bastion hosts with a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone
Replace the three bastion hosts with one larger bastion host in a single Availability Zone
explanation: Session Manager provides IAM-controlled, audited shell access to private instances without bastion hosts, open inbound ports, or Elastic IP addresses, so the bastion instances and their public IPv4 charges can be removed. A single larger bastion still costs money and becomes a single point of failure. Public subnets increase exposure. NAT gateways provide outbound internet access rather than inbound administrative access, and they are billed hourly.

question: A company installed the CloudWatch agent on 2,000 instances in Auto Scaling groups to collect memory and disk metrics. Because each metric includes the InstanceId dimension and instances are replaced often, the number of custom metrics and the CloudWatch bill are much higher than expected. The operations team needs only fleet-level values per Auto Scaling group. Which change will reduce cost while meeting the requirement?
options: Reduce the agent's metric collection interval to 1 second
Configure the agent to send the metrics to an S3 bucket instead of CloudWatch
Enable detailed monitoring on all of the instances
Configure the agent to publish the metrics with only the AutoScalingGroupName dimension instead of per-instance dimensions
explanation: CloudWatch bills for each unique custom metric, which is defined by its name and dimension combination, so per-instance dimensions on a frequently replaced fleet create a large number of metrics. Publishing the metrics with only the AutoScalingGroupName dimension provides group-level values with far fewer custom metrics. Detailed monitoring adds cost for the default metrics, a 1-second interval increases API requests and cost, and the agent does not publish metrics to S3.

question: A company runs a production web application in a load-balanced AWS Elastic Beanstalk environment. Deployments must never reduce serving capacity, a failed deployment must leave the instances that run the current version untouched, and rollback must be as quick and safe as possible without any DNS change. Which deployment policy should the company use?
options: Immutable
Rolling
All at once
Rolling with additional batch
explanation: An immutable deployment launches a full set of new instances in a separate Auto Scaling group; if they fail health checks, Elastic Beanstalk terminates them and the original instances keep serving, so rollback is simply terminating the new instances. All at once causes downtime. Rolling takes batches out of service and reduces capacity. Rolling with additional batch keeps capacity but updates existing instances, so a failure after some batches leaves a mix of versions that must be fixed by a manual redeploy.

question: A company runs 20 instances in a load-balanced AWS Elastic Beanstalk environment. During deployments the environment must keep its full capacity of 20 instances serving traffic. To control cost, the company does not want to run a second full set of 20 instances during each deployment, and a longer deployment time is acceptable. Which deployment policy meets these requirements?
options: Immutable
Rolling with additional batch
Traffic splitting
Rolling
explanation: Rolling with additional batch first launches one extra batch of instances and then deploys batch by batch, so full capacity is kept while only one batch of extra instances runs at a time; the extra batch is terminated when the deployment completes. Immutable and traffic-splitting deployments launch a full new set of instances equal to the current fleet. A plain rolling deployment takes each batch out of service and reduces capacity.
subtopic: Elastic Beanstalk rolling with additional batch

question: A company must move an AWS Elastic Beanstalk application to a new platform branch with a newer major runtime version, which is not compatible with an in-place platform update. The company wants to test the new version with production-like settings and switch users over with minimal downtime, and it must be able to switch back quickly. Which approach meets these requirements?
options: Enable managed platform updates with the minor and patch update level
Change the deployment policy to traffic splitting and update the platform version in place
Clone the environment onto the new platform version, test it, and then swap the environment URLs (CNAMEs) of the two environments
Use the all at once deployment policy and redeploy the previous version if problems occur
explanation: A blue/green deployment is required for an incompatible platform version: run the new version in a separate environment, test it, and swap the environment CNAMEs to redirect traffic; swapping back returns users to the old environment, which should be kept until DNS caches expire. Managed platform updates apply only patch and minor updates within a platform branch. Traffic splitting and all at once are deployment policies for application versions within the same environment, and all at once causes downtime.

question: A team deploys a new application version to an AWS Elastic Beanstalk environment that uses an Application Load Balancer. The team wants to send 10% of client traffic to the new version for 15 minutes, automatically shift all traffic to it if it stays healthy, and automatically move traffic back to the old version if it does not. Which deployment policy should the team configure?
options: Rolling with a batch size of 10%
Immutable with a health check threshold of Warning
All at once with enhanced health reporting
Traffic splitting with a 10% traffic split and a 15-minute evaluation time
explanation: Traffic-splitting deployments launch a full set of new instances, forward a configured percentage of traffic to them for an evaluation period, and then either shift all traffic to the new version or move traffic back and terminate the new instances; this canary pattern requires an Application Load Balancer. A rolling deployment with 10% batches updates existing instances and does not control the share of client traffic. Immutable deployments do not send a defined fraction of traffic for evaluation, and all at once causes downtime.

question: Developers deploy to an AWS Elastic Beanstalk development environment dozens of times a day. They want the fastest possible deployments and do not want to pay for any extra instances during deployments. Brief interruptions in the development environment are acceptable. Which deployment policy should they use?
options: All at once
Immutable
Rolling with additional batch
Traffic splitting
explanation: All at once deploys the new version to all existing instances simultaneously, which is the quickest method and launches no extra instances, at the cost of a short loss of service. Immutable and traffic splitting launch a full set of new instances and are the slowest policies. Rolling with additional batch launches an extra batch and takes longer than a plain rolling deployment.
subtopic: Elastic Beanstalk all at once deployments

question: A web application on AWS Elastic Beanstalk generates PDF reports and resizes uploaded images inside web requests, which makes the site slow under load. The company wants the web tier to stay responsive, the background work to scale independently, and nightly cleanup jobs to run on a schedule, with the LEAST custom infrastructure code. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Increase the instance size of the web environment and enable sticky sessions on the load balancer
Create an Elastic Beanstalk worker environment; have the web tier send tasks to the worker environment's Amazon SQS queue and define the nightly jobs in a cron.yaml file
Run the background tasks as cron jobs on every web server instance by using .ebextensions
Add a second web server environment and use Route 53 weighted routing to send report requests to it
explanation: An Elastic Beanstalk worker environment manages an Amazon SQS queue and runs a daemon that pulls messages and posts them to the application, so long-running tasks are decoupled from the web tier and scale separately; periodic tasks are defined in cron.yaml. Larger web instances still process the work inside requests. Cron jobs on every web instance compete with user traffic and run duplicate jobs. A second web environment behind weighted routing still processes the work synchronously.

question: A company's AWS Elastic Beanstalk environment includes an Amazon RDS DB instance that Elastic Beanstalk created as part of the environment. The company now wants to use blue/green deployments for major releases without losing or disrupting the production database. Which actions should a solutions architect recommend? (Select TWO.)
options: Run the production database independently of the environment, for example by decoupling it with the Retain option or using a standalone RDS instance, and point both environments to it
Enable Multi-AZ on the Elastic Beanstalk-created database so that it moves to the green environment automatically
Switch to the all at once deployment policy so that the database is updated together with the application
Clone the environment, deploy and test the new version in the clone, and then swap the environment URLs
Terminate the blue environment immediately after the URL swap so that DNS changes propagate faster
explanation: Blue/green deployments require the environments to run independently of the production database, so a database created inside the environment should be decoupled (for example with the Retain lifecycle option) or replaced by a standalone RDS instance that both environments use. The release is then deployed to a cloned environment and traffic is moved by swapping environment URLs. Multi-AZ does not move a database between environments, all at once is not a blue/green method, and the old environment should be kept until DNS records cached by clients have expired.

question: A security policy requires that every AWS Elastic Beanstalk production environment receives operating system and runtime security patches within a week of their release, without reducing serving capacity and without engineers performing manual updates. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Create a cron job on each instance that runs the package manager's update command every night
Use AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager to patch the Elastic Beanstalk instances in place every week
Enable managed platform updates with a weekly maintenance window, which applies patch and minor platform updates through immutable updates
Rebuild the environment from scratch every week by using a saved configuration
explanation: Managed platform updates automatically upgrade an environment to the latest patch or minor platform version during a weekly maintenance window, and they always use immutable updates so the application stays in service with no reduction in capacity. In-place patching with cron or Patch Manager changes instances outside Elastic Beanstalk's control, and patched instances are replaced by unpatched ones when the environment scales. Rebuilding environments weekly is manual and disruptive.

question: Which AWS Elastic Beanstalk deployment policies deploy the new application version only to newly launched instances instead of updating instances that are already serving traffic? (Select TWO.)
options: All at once
Immutable
Rolling
Rolling with additional batch
Traffic splitting
explanation: Immutable and traffic-splitting deployments launch a fresh set of instances for the new version and terminate the old instances only after the new ones are healthy, which gives a fast and safe rollback. All at once and rolling deploy to existing instances. Rolling with additional batch deploys to the extra batch of new instances and also to existing instances.

question: A startup uses AWS Elastic Beanstalk for an internal tool that has a handful of users and for several developer test environments. The startup wants to minimize the monthly cost of these environments and does not need automatic scaling. Which configuration is MOST cost-effective?
options: Load-balanced environments with a minimum of two instances in different Availability Zones
Worker environments, which do not include a load balancer
Load-balanced environments that use the traffic-splitting deployment policy
Single-instance environments, which run one instance with an Elastic IP address and no load balancer
explanation: A single-instance environment runs one EC2 instance with an Elastic IP address and has no load balancer, which reduces cost for low-traffic and development workloads; it can be changed to a load-balanced environment later. Elastic Beanstalk itself has no additional charge, so cost comes from the resources it creates. Load-balanced environments add load balancer charges and more instances. A worker environment processes queue messages and cannot serve web traffic.

question: A stateless API runs in a load-balanced AWS Elastic Beanstalk environment that scales between 4 and 24 instances. The company wants to cut compute costs with Spot Instances but must always keep at least 4 On-Demand Instances and wants half of any capacity above that to be On-Demand. Which configuration meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Enable Spot Instances in the environment's capacity settings with an On-Demand base of 4 and an On-Demand above base percentage of 50
Create a separate Spot Fleet outside Elastic Beanstalk and register its instances with the environment's load balancer
Purchase 1-year Reserved Instances to cover the maximum of 24 instances
Create two Elastic Beanstalk environments, one On-Demand and one Spot, and split traffic with Route 53 weighted records
explanation: Elastic Beanstalk can launch a mix of On-Demand and Spot Instances in the environment's Auto Scaling group by using EnableSpot, SpotFleetOnDemandBase, and SpotFleetOnDemandAboveBasePercentage, so a base of 4 On-Demand Instances with 50% On-Demand above the base meets the requirement natively; Capacity Rebalancing can further reduce interruption impact. A separate Spot Fleet or two environments add infrastructure to manage, and Reserved Instances sized for the maximum of 24 instances would pay for capacity that is idle most of the time.

question: An EC2 Image Builder pipeline produces a new hardened AMI every week. Auto Scaling groups in two application accounts reference launch templates, and engineers currently update each launch template by hand after every build, which sometimes leaves groups launching outdated images. Which solution automates this with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Use AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager to patch the running instances so that the AMI does not need to change
Add launch template configurations to the pipeline's distribution settings so that Image Builder creates a new launch template version with the new AMI ID and sets it as the default
Write a Lambda function that polls for new AMIs and updates the Auto Scaling groups to use the AMI ID directly
Share the AMI with the organization and ask each team to update its launch templates after receiving an email notification
explanation: Image Builder distribution settings can include launch template configurations; for each build, Image Builder creates a new launch template version that contains the new AMI ID and can set it as the default version, including for launch templates in other accounts through its cross-account distribution role. Auto Scaling groups that use the default version then launch the new image. Patching instances in place does not change what new instances launch with. A custom Lambda function or manual updates add maintenance and risk.

question: An Auto Scaling group was created with version 3 of a launch template selected explicitly. An engineer created version 4 with a patched AMI and set it as the template's default version, but instances launched during scale-out still use the old AMI. What should the engineer do so that the group uses the new AMI?
options: Modify version 3 of the launch template in place to reference the patched AMI
Reboot all instances in the group so that they load the new default version
Update the Auto Scaling group to use the launch template's default (or latest) version, and then replace the existing instances, for example with an instance refresh
Wait for the new default version to propagate to the Auto Scaling group, which can take up to 24 hours
explanation: An Auto Scaling group uses the default version, the latest version, or a specific version of a launch template, as configured on the group; because this group pins version 3, changing the template's default has no effect until the group is set to use the default or latest version (or version 4). Existing instances keep their original configuration until they are replaced, for example by an instance refresh. Launch template versions are immutable, rebooting does not change the AMI of an instance, and there is no propagation delay.

question: A company requires that an endpoint protection agent be installed and running on every managed EC2 instance, including instances launched by Auto Scaling in the future. Operators sometimes stop the service while troubleshooting and forget to restart it. Which solution keeps the instances compliant with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Install the agent in the AMI and rely on the operators to restart it after troubleshooting
Use Run Command once a month to reinstall the agent on all instances
Add the installation script to the user data of every launch template
Create an AWS Systems Manager State Manager association that targets the instances by tag and runs on a schedule to install the agent if it is missing and start the service if it is stopped
explanation: State Manager associations define a desired state, target nodes by tags or other criteria, and are reapplied on a schedule, so the agent is installed on new instances and restarted if it is found stopped, correcting configuration drift automatically. Baking the agent into the AMI or user data covers only the first boot. A monthly Run Command leaves long gaps and must be triggered by someone.

question: A company runs 15 critical instances of a quorum-based service. Each instance must run on distinct hardware so that a single rack failure affects at most one instance, and the service must also survive the loss of an Availability Zone. The Region has three Availability Zones. Which placement configuration meets these requirements?
options: A single spread placement group that spans the three Availability Zones, with five instances in each Availability Zone
A single cluster placement group in one Availability Zone
A partition placement group with one partition in one Availability Zone
A single spread placement group with all 15 instances in one Availability Zone
explanation: A rack-level spread placement group places each instance on a distinct rack and can span multiple Availability Zones in a Region, with a maximum of seven running instances per Availability Zone, so five instances in each of three AZs fits and also survives an AZ loss. Fifteen instances in one AZ exceed the spread limit and do not survive an AZ failure. A cluster placement group concentrates instances in one AZ, and a single partition does not separate the instances from each other.

question: A developer can launch EC2 instances but receives an authorization error whenever the developer tries to launch an instance with the instance profile AppServerProfile, which contains the role AppServerRole. Following least privilege, which permission should an administrator add to the developer's IAM policy?
options: iam:CreateRole on all resources
iam:PassRole on the ARN of AppServerRole
sts:AssumeRole on the ARN of AppServerRole
iam:* on all roles in the account
explanation: Launching an instance with an IAM role, or attaching or replacing a role, requires iam:PassRole for that role, and least privilege means scoping the permission to the specific role ARN rather than using a wildcard. The developer does not need to create roles or assume the role; the EC2 service delivers the role credentials to the instance. iam:* grants far more access than required.

question: A company wants AWS Systems Manager to manage every current and future EC2 instance in an account, so that Session Manager, Patch Manager, and Inventory work, without attaching an IAM instance profile to each instance. The instances run a recent version of SSM Agent. Which actions are required? (Select TWO.)
options: Assign a public IPv4 address to every instance so that it can register with Systems Manager
Allow inbound HTTPS from the Systems Manager service in each instance security group
Turn on Default Host Management Configuration in each AWS Region where the instances run
Attach the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy to an instance profile on every instance
Configure the instances to use IMDSv2, because Default Host Management Configuration does not support IMDSv1
explanation: Default Host Management Configuration lets Systems Manager manage EC2 instances by applying a default IAM role at the account and Region level, so no per-instance instance profile is needed; it must be turned on in each Region, and managed instances must use IMDSv2 and a supported SSM Agent version. SSM Agent makes outbound connections, so no inbound rules or public IP addresses are required, and attaching instance profiles is exactly what the company wants to avoid.

question: Database administrators need to connect from their laptops with a SQL client to an Amazon RDS for MySQL instance in a private subnet. The company does not allow bastion hosts with open SSH ports or public IP addresses, and every connection must be authorized through IAM. A managed EC2 instance with SSM Agent already runs in the same VPC. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Make the RDS instance publicly accessible and restrict its security group to the administrators' IP addresses
Create a Site-to-Site VPN connection from each laptop to the VPC
Start a Session Manager port forwarding session to the remote host by using the AWS-StartPortForwardingSessionToRemoteHost document through the managed instance
Open TCP port 22 on the managed instance and use SSH tunneling with a shared key
explanation: Session Manager can forward a local port through a managed node to a remote host such as an RDS endpoint by using the AWS-StartPortForwardingSessionToRemoteHost document; access is controlled with IAM and no inbound ports or bastion host are needed, while the remote host does not have to be a managed node. Making the database public or opening SSH violates the requirements, and per-laptop VPN connections are not a practical or IAM-controlled solution.

question: Support engineers occasionally need a graphical Remote Desktop session to Windows Server EC2 instances in private subnets. The security team will not allow inbound RDP (TCP 3389) in any security group, bastion hosts, or VPN clients. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Use EC2 Instance Connect to push a temporary RDP certificate to each instance
Associate Elastic IP addresses with the instances and allow RDP only from the support office
Deploy a Network Load Balancer that forwards TCP 3389 to the instances
Use AWS Systems Manager Fleet Manager Remote Desktop to connect to the managed instances from the Systems Manager console
explanation: Fleet Manager Remote Desktop provides browser-based RDP connections to Windows Server managed instances through Session Manager, so no inbound ports need to be opened, and access is governed by IAM. EC2 Instance Connect is for SSH, not RDP. Elastic IP addresses and a load balancer both require exposing port 3389, which the security team prohibits.

question: After a library vulnerability is announced, a security team must identify every EC2 instance across 40 AWS accounts and several Regions that has a specific version of the library installed. The team wants to run SQL queries against a central dataset and keep it updated automatically. All instances are Systems Manager managed nodes. Which actions should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)
options: Configure Systems Manager Inventory to collect application inventory from the managed nodes
Run a script over SSH in every account that writes package lists to a shared spreadsheet
Create resource data syncs that send inventory data to a central Amazon S3 bucket, and query the data with Amazon Athena
Enable AWS CloudTrail data events for EC2 and search them with CloudTrail Lake
Use AWS Trusted Advisor checks to list the installed software on each instance
explanation: Systems Manager Inventory collects software and configuration metadata from managed nodes, and a resource data sync automatically delivers that data from multiple accounts and Regions to a central S3 bucket, where Amazon Athena can query it with SQL. SSH scripts are manual and need open ports. CloudTrail records API activity, not installed packages, and Trusted Advisor does not inventory software inside instances.

question: A company with AWS Organizations must scan all managed EC2 instances in 60 accounts and 4 Regions for missing patches every day and install approved patches every Sunday night. The company wants a single configuration to manage instead of maintenance windows in every account and Region pair. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Create a Quick Setup patch policy for the organization that specifies the patch baselines, a daily scan schedule, and a weekly install schedule
Create a maintenance window and patch group in each account and Region by using CloudFormation StackSets
Use AWS Config conformance packs to install missing patches
Use EC2 Image Builder to rebuild every instance with the latest patches each week
explanation: Patch policies in Quick Setup let one configuration apply patching to all managed nodes across accounts, Regions, or selected organizational units, with separate scan and install schedules and a selected patch baseline per operating system, and they run AWS-RunPatchBaseline. Per-account maintenance windows work but create many resources to maintain. AWS Config evaluates compliance but does not install patches, and rebuilding images does not patch running instances.

question: A company uses AWS Systems Manager Session Manager for shell access. Developers must be able to start sessions only on instances tagged Environment=dev and must be able to end only their own sessions, while production instances remain off limits. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Create separate VPCs for development and production and block Session Manager endpoints in the production VPC

Attach an IAM policy that allows ssm:StartSession on instances with the condition ssm:resourceTag/Environment equal to dev, and allows ssm:TerminateSession only on sessions that begin with the user's ID
Change the security groups of production instances to deny inbound traffic from the developers' IP addresses
Remove the SSM Agent from production instances so that they cannot be reached
explanation: Session Manager access is controlled with IAM; ssm:StartSession can be limited to instances whose tags match by using the ssm:resourceTag condition key, and ssm:TerminateSession can be restricted to session resources prefixed with the caller's user ID. Security groups do not affect Session Manager because the agent connects outbound. Removing the agent or blocking endpoints breaks management of production instances instead of enforcing least privilege.

question: Operations engineers use an AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook to stop a production database instance, create an AMI, and restart it. Change management now requires that two members of a change advisory board approve each run before the instance is stopped, and approvers must be notified automatically. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Ask the approvers to reply to an email and have the engineer start the runbook after receiving two replies
Store the approval in a Parameter Store parameter that the runbook reads before stopping the instance
Add an aws:approve step at the start of the runbook with the two approvers, MinRequiredApprovals set to 2, and an Amazon SNS topic for notifications
Require the engineers to run the steps manually through Session Manager while an approver watches the session
explanation: The aws:approve action pauses an automation until the required number of designated principals approve or reject it, sends the request to an SNS topic, and resumes only after approval, which enforces the control inside the runbook. Email replies and manual supervision depend on people following a process and are not enforced. A parameter that anyone with write access can change is not a reliable approval record.

question: A company wants to add an existing EBS-backed EC2 instance to a cluster placement group with other HPC nodes. What must be done to move the instance into the placement group?
options: Create an AMI and launch a new instance, because instances can never be moved into a placement group
Detach the instance's network interface and attach it to an instance in the placement group
Modify the placement of the running instance; the change applies without stopping it
Stop the instance, change its placement group with the modify instance placement action, and then start it
explanation: An instance must be in the stopped state before it can be added to, moved between, or removed from a placement group, which is done with the Modify instance placement action or the modify-instance-placement command, after which the instance is started. The placement cannot be changed while the instance is running. Relaunching from an AMI is unnecessary, and moving a network interface does not move the instance.

question: A data replication service copies large datasets between two supported EC2 instances in different Availability Zones of the same Region over a single TCP connection. Each instance has 50 Gbps of aggregate bandwidth, but the transfer never exceeds about 5 Gbps. Which change will MOST increase the throughput of this single flow?
options: Enable ENA Express on the network interface attachments of both instances so that the flow uses AWS Scalable Reliable Datagram (SRD)
Move both instances into a cluster placement group
Attach a second elastic network interface to each instance
Enable EBS optimization on both instances
explanation: ENA Express uses SRD to raise the maximum bandwidth of a single flow from 5 Gbps to up to 25 Gbps between supported instances in the same Region, including across Availability Zones, when it is enabled on both the sender and the receiver. A cluster placement group raises single-flow traffic only to 10 Gbps and cannot span Availability Zones. A second network interface does not raise the per-flow limit, and EBS optimization affects storage traffic, not instance-to-instance traffic.

question: A CloudFormation template launches Amazon Linux 2023 instances, and engineers must edit the hardcoded AMI ID in every Region whenever AWS releases a new image. The company wants the template to always use the latest Amazon Linux 2023 AMI in any Region without maintaining a mapping. What should a solutions architect do?
options: Use AWS Compute Optimizer to look up the AMI ID during stack creation
Reference the AWS public parameter under /aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/ in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store
Copy the latest AMI into every Region each month and update a Mappings section
Store the AMI ID in the instance user data and update it after launch
explanation: AWS publishes public Parameter Store parameters for the latest Amazon Linux AMIs in each Region under /aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/, so templates and launch templates can reference the parameter instead of a hardcoded AMI ID. Maintaining mappings or copies is manual work. Compute Optimizer gives right-sizing recommendations, and user data runs after the instance has already been launched from an AMI.

question: When an Auto Scaling group launches 150 instances during a traffic spike, many instances fail to start their application because GetParameter calls to AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store return ThrottlingException errors. Each instance reads the same 12 parameters one at a time every few seconds. Which actions will resolve the issue? (Select TWO.)
options: Move all parameters to the advanced tier, which removes the throughput limit
Enable the Parameter Store higher throughput setting for the account and Region
Convert the parameters to SecureString parameters
Cache parameter values in the application and retrieve the known parameters together with a single GetParameters call
Store the parameters in the user data of the launch template
explanation: Parameter Store has a default shared throughput quota for GetParameter, GetParameters, and GetParametersByPath, and enabling higher throughput raises it for the account and Region at an additional per-interaction charge. Reducing calls by caching values and fetching several known parameters with one GetParameters request also avoids throttling. Parameter tiers control size limits and policies, not throughput, and SecureString only adds encryption. User data is not designed for configuration that changes and is readable by anyone who can view instance attributes.

question: A legacy application on EC2 runs a background Java process that sometimes crashes silently while the instance stays healthy, and the operations team also needs to track that process's memory usage over time. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST effort?
options: Enable detailed monitoring and alarm on the CPUUtilization metric
Create an EC2 status check alarm with the reboot action
Configure the procstat plugin of the CloudWatch agent to collect metrics such as pid_count and memory_rss for the process, and create an alarm when pid_count drops to zero
Enable VPC Flow Logs and alarm when traffic from the process stops
explanation: The CloudWatch agent procstat plugin collects metrics for individual processes selected by PID file, executable name, or command-line pattern, including pid_count and memory_rss, so an alarm can fire when the process is not running and memory can be tracked over time. Status checks and CPUUtilization reflect the instance, not a specific process. Flow Logs record network traffic metadata and are an unreliable signal for a background process.

question: A research team runs containerized jobs with AWS Batch. AWS recommends Fargate compute environments for most Batch workloads. Which job requirements would require the team to use an Amazon EC2 compute environment instead of Fargate? (Select TWO.)
options: Jobs that need a GPU
Jobs that need 4 vCPUs and 16 GiB of memory
Jobs that must start within about a minute of being submitted
Jobs that need an IAM role to read input files from Amazon S3
Jobs that must run on a custom Amazon Machine Image (AMI)
explanation: AWS Batch guidance recommends EC2 compute environments when jobs need a GPU, a custom AMI, more than 32 vCPUs, more than 244 GiB of memory, or certain Linux parameters. A job with 4 vCPUs and 16 GiB fits Fargate, Fargate jobs typically start faster than new EC2 instances, and both compute environment types support IAM roles for jobs.

question: A company runs thousands of short containerized data-processing jobs each day with AWS Batch on a managed EC2 compute environment. Each job needs 2 vCPUs and 4 GiB of memory, and no job needs a GPU or a custom AMI. The instances are often underutilized between job bursts, and the team spends time tuning instance types. Which change will MOST reduce cost and operational effort?
options: Switch to an unmanaged EC2 compute environment and pack jobs onto instances manually
Purchase EC2 Instance Savings Plans for the instance types used by the compute environment
Increase the minimum vCPUs of the compute environment so that instances are always warm
Move the jobs to an AWS Batch Fargate compute environment so that capacity matches each job's requested vCPU and memory
explanation: With Fargate, AWS Batch provisions compute that closely matches the CPU and memory each job requests, so there are no instances to choose, scale, or over-provision, and jobs can typically start in about 30 seconds. These jobs do not need a GPU, a custom AMI, or large sizes that would require EC2. Unmanaged environments add operational work, a higher minimum keeps idle capacity running, and a Savings Plan discounts underutilized instances without removing the waste.
